article.overview: A cryogenic sample preservation system keeps collected lunar material at low temperature inside controlled containment, so that volatile components, such as water ice and other compounds that readily leave a solid, are not lost or chemically altered between collection and laboratory analysis. NASA authors state that samples from permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) are cryogenic when collected, so lunar polar sample return will eventually require cold stowage [1]. The NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) curation office describes cold curation capability for Artemis samples as an area under active development [4]. No flown lunar cryogenic preservation system with published specifications was identified. The catalogue category name refers to detection, whereas this payload preserves samples, so the link to volatile-bearing material is a functional relationship rather than a category match.
article.description: The payload would receive or collect a sample, hold it inside a sealed and thermally controlled enclosure, and keep it below a defined temperature for a defined period. NASA ground work uses analog temperatures to define the requirement. In the JSC study of volatile-bearing simulants, -20 °C is the analog for Apollo cold-curated samples, -80 °C is the temperature of several flight payload freezers, and -196 °C is analogous to lunar PSRs [1]. Work at the JSC Planetary Exploration and Astromaterials Research Laboratory (PEARL) on cryogenic regolith simulants describes working temperatures at or below -196 °C [2]. A preservation system addresses the period between collection and analysis rather than the measurement itself. It is distinct from the analytical instruments in the same catalogue category, which determine what volatile material is present, and from historical sample containers, which were designed to contain and protect samples rather than to control their temperature.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main scientific purpose is to preserve samples so that later measurements represent the material as it was collected. NASA's Astromaterials curation office states that its responsibility includes the documentation, preservation and preparation of samples from the Moon, and that its highest priority is to secure the future availability of these samples for the worldwide scientific community [5]. A cryogenic system would extend this principle to volatile-bearing material. Calaway and Allen argue that several sample types, including cometary, asteroidal, meteoritic and subsurface lunar material, were cold before collection, and that warming them to room temperature on Earth can erase valuable volatile chemistry. They conclude that storing, documenting, subdividing and transporting such samples at subfreezing or cryogenic temperatures is needed for complete study [3]. Potential applications include laboratory analysis of volatile composition, comparison with in-situ measurements at the collection site, and long-term curation of temperature-sensitive samples. Whether usable volatile-bearing material will be collected is a scientific question that the sources do not answer.
article.operating_principle: No published operating principle for a specific lunar cryogenic sample preservation system was found. The following is design reasoning rather than a documented design. The enclosure would need to (1) contain the sample in a sealed or controlled atmosphere, (2) limit heat flow into the sample, typically through insulation and either a cold reservoir or an active cooler, (3) measure the sample temperature with sensors logged against a time reference, and (4) avoid contamination and mechanical disturbance during handling. The JSC team's stated goal for its temperature study is to define the temperatures needed for a flight cold stowage freezer [1]. The JSC curation abstract says that facilities and procedures are being designed using practices from the cold and cryogenic sample industries [4]. Lewis and co-authors note that handling cryogenic simulants needs new procedures and engineering because of the extreme cold [2]. The cooling method, temperature set-point and control architecture are not publicly specified in the verified sources. A terrestrial precedent exists for atmosphere control, not temperature control. Apollo-era samples are handled in nitrogen-purged, glove-operated cabinets [7].
article.scientific_importance: Sample curation is central to lunar science because the Apollo collection remains a basis for research. Six Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972 returned 382 kilograms of lunar rocks, cores, pebbles, sand and dust, comprising about 2,200 separate samples [6]. Continued research depends on the condition of those samples. For volatile-bearing material, loss of volatile species during return and storage could change the scientific interpretation of a sample [1][3]. The importance of a cryogenic preservation approach is therefore conditional. JSC expects that Artemis samples from PSRs and other cold environments will contain ices and volatile components that need sub-zero or cryogenic handling [4]. That is an expectation stated in a planning abstract, not a measured result.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a cryogenic sample preservation system. The catalogue entry describes a function, not a flown instrument. Mass, dimensions, power, cooling capacity, sealing performance and lifetime for a specific lunar cryogenic sample preservation system were not verified in the sources reviewed. The two examples below are a procurement-stage NASA freezer concept, whose values come mainly from secondary summaries, and a non-cryogenic Apollo handling facility included only as a functional baseline.

examples.name: NASA Lunar Freezer System (procurement stage, not built)
examples.type: Proposed, contracted development; no built or flight-ready hardware described
examples.description:
Search-result summaries of a NASA request for information describe a freezer intended to store materials brought back from the Moon. A contract article dated 5 December 2025 reports that NASA awarded an indefinite-delivery contract to the University of Alabama at Birmingham's Engineering and Innovative Technology Development group, with a potential total value of $37 million, a 66-month base period starting 4 December 2025 and options through June 2033, to develop and manage a Lunar Freezer System [8]. The article states that the system must operate aboard the Orion spacecraft or potential commercial return vehicles, and that the contractor will "design, build, and certify" the hardware. No built or flight-ready hardware is described [8]. The same article gives a temperature range of "likely in the -85°C range", which is the author's estimate and not a stated requirement [8].

Secondary summaries of the NASA request for information report a requirement that lunar samples stay at or below -150 °C, and biological samples at or below -80 °C. They also report stowage targets of 1 to 3 weeks for passive solutions and 10 to 90 or more days for powered solutions [9]. Search-result aggregator pages report a cold interior of no less than about 25 × 25 × 66 cm and a total system mass below 55 kg. These figures were not checked against the primary notice and should be treated as unverified. Reported readiness for Artemis 5 by the end of 2027 also comes from summaries and has not been confirmed.
examples.reported_stowage_duration_secondary_summ: 1 to 3 weeks (passive solutions); 10 to 90 or more days (powered solutions)
examples.qualification: Contracted development. Hardware not described as built, tested or flight-qualified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Apollo Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility handling (non-cryogenic baseline)
examples.type: Historical sample-handling facility; not a cryogenic payload
examples.description: The Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility at the Johnson Space Center opened in 1979 to house the Apollo samples [7]. Researchers prepare samples in stainless steel cabinets through multi-layered gloves. The cabinet atmosphere is purged with high-purity nitrogen and is continuously monitored for oxygen and moisture content, and the laboratory and vault air is kept at slightly higher than atmospheric pressure [7]. The sources reviewed describe no temperature-controlled storage for this facility. This example is a containment and atmosphere baseline only. It is not a cryogenic system, and no numerical mass, dimension or power values apply.
examples.temperature_control: No temperature-controlled storage described in the sources reviewed.
examples.atmosphere_control: High-purity nitrogen purge in glove-operated stainless steel cabinets, with oxygen and moisture continuously monitored. No numerical values reported in the source.
examples.qualification: Facility practice described in a secondary source. No numerical specifications apply.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions and proportions are not publicly specified for any verified cryogenic preservation hardware. The procurement-stage cold interior dimensions in Example 1 come from unverified summaries. An enclosure would need to be sized to the sample volume and to the insulation, cooling and mounting interfaces of its host system.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is normally expressed in kilograms for spacecraft and lander interfaces. The procurement-stage limit of under 55 kg in Example 1 is unverified, and the enclosure mass would also include insulation, cooling hardware and control electronics.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified. Secondary search summaries cite a practical power ceiling of about 200 W for Orion and the Human Landing System and up to about 600 W for Gateway. These values are unverified and were not checked against primary interface documents. Any active cooling would need a power budget that depends on heat leak, holding time and cooler efficiency.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A cryogenic sample preservation system would have to operate across each environment the sample passes through: the collection site, any transfer or launch environment, the return chain and the laboratory. The laboratory side is documented in part. Apollo-era cabinets are nitrogen-purged and monitored for oxygen and moisture [7]. For the lunar-surface and transit side, the verified sources give analog temperatures and planning intentions rather than interface requirements. The planned JSC test stores volatile-bearing regolith analogs at several temperatures for two weeks and analyses the headspace gas, to define the temperatures needed for a flight freezer [1]. The same study expects composition and morphology changes in samples above 0 °C [1]. Secondary summaries report that containment must stay at or below -150 °C through roughly two weeks of transfers, with limits on space, power and cryocooler life on each vehicle. These statements have not been verified against primary NASA documents. Vibration and shock tolerance, holding time and data interfaces are not publicly specified.
article.limitations: Several limitations apply. First, no flown or flight-qualified lunar cryogenic sample preservation system was identified, so this article cannot describe demonstrated performance. Second, the ground tests that would define the temperature requirement were described as planned, and no measured volatile-loss results were retrieved. Third, the cited temperature targets are not consistent across sources: -150 °C for lunar samples and -80 °C for biological samples are reported in secondary summaries, -85 °C is an author estimate, and -196 °C is an analog for PSR conditions. Fourth, cooling on the Moon requires a sustained power source and a thermal path to a cold reservoir, and both constrain mass, volume and lander interfaces. Fifth, sealing a volatile-bearing sample from collection through return is difficult, and a leak would defeat the purpose. Sixth, cold storage does not prevent all change, because samples can alter during collection, handling and warm-up for analysis.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A cryogenic sample preservation system would most plausibly sit inside a sample-return chain or a surface sample-handling chain, rather than being a standalone orbiting payload. The sample-return constraints relevant here are containment, handling, sealing, transfer and the return-chain temperature budget. The contract article states that the Lunar Freezer System is to operate aboard Orion or potential commercial return vehicles [8]. Secondary summaries report that collection to splashdown takes about two weeks across several vehicles, and that the freezer's stowage limits differ between the Human Landing System, Gateway and Orion [9]. These statements describe intended operation. Compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft has not been verified against interface documents, and none is asserted here.
transportation_process: Integrate the preservation enclosure and its thermal control hardware into the sample-collection or sample-handling system on Earth, with thermal and contamination requirements defined.
Launch with the spacecraft, which requires the enclosure to be qualified for launch loads and vacuum. Launch-qualification values are not publicly specified.
Transfer through cruise or lunar transfer, keeping the preservation chain powered or passively insulated as the mission design allows.
Land with the lander or ascent and return vehicle, subject to landing loads and thermal limits. These limits are not publicly specified for any named vehicle.

Deploy or operate the system on the surface, or transfer the sample into it: collect or receive the sample, seal the enclosure and maintain the target temperature, with power and data interfaces defined by the host vehicle.
For return, maintain containment and temperature through the return chain, then handle the sample in a controlled laboratory environment on arrival.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Possible approaches include a manipulator-based transfer from a sampling device into a sealed enclosure, or a fixed system that receives sample material in situ. The sources reviewed do not describe a verified method for a specific mission. The choice would depend on the host platform, the sample form and the thermal design. A freezer used as a stowage element inside a vehicle is a different deployment case from a surface device, and the sources do not settle which will be used.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No cryogenic sample preservation system has been documented as flown. Apollo samples were returned and curated without cryogenic stowage, and were handled in nitrogen-purged cabinets [7]. NASA's Astromaterials curation office continues to curate lunar samples [5][6]. JSC describes cold curation capability as under development for Artemis samples [4]. The procurement-stage freezer described in Example 1 is the closest current programmatic example [8][9].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any lander, rover or spacecraft has not been assessed in this article, because no verified interface specifications were retrieved. The contract article's statement that the system is intended for Orion or commercial return vehicles [8] is a stated intent and does not establish interface compatibility. A full assessment would need mass, volume, power, thermal interface, mounting, sample-transfer method, data interface and landing environment, compared against verified host-vehicle documentation.

article.historical_significance: A cryogenic sample preservation system is not documented as having flown or been tested in the sources reviewed. Its historical context is the Apollo curation programme, which returned 382 kilograms of samples [6], and the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility, which opened in 1979 [7]. Since 2011, the concept has moved from a conceptual argument for cold curation [3], to ground-test planning [1], to dedicated laboratory capability for cryogenic simulants [2], to a JSC curation development effort [4], and to a contracted freezer procurement [8][9]. This progression shows growing programmatic commitment. It does not establish that a flight-qualified system exists.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: This article rests on a limited source set. Several NASA technical PDFs (the Mitchell et al. 2022 full paper, the Lewis et al. 2023 poster, the Calaway and Allen 2011 full paper, and the Harrington et al. 2026 record) were returned as binary content and could not be read as text, so claims from them rely on abstracts or summaries. Two pages returned HTTP 403 and were not read: a Georgia Tech repository record on cryogenic lunar sample return, and a Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) conference presentation page. A JAXA curation target below -110 °C for samples from the lunar south pole appeared only in a search summary and is not verified. The Space.com article on the lunar freezer returned its headline only. The procurement-stage figures in Example 1 are unverified, and the SAM.gov notices were not checked. Artemis schedules and vehicle plans may have changed since the source documents were written. The Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility source is a Wikipedia article read through a fetch summariser, so its specific statements should be checked against NASA curation documents before use. No direct image assets were verified, and no image is included. No mass, dimensions, power, temperature, sealing, lifetime or qualification value is given for any verified cryogenic preservation hardware. The association with volatile detection is inferred from the catalogue category name, and the catalogue category does not describe a preservation function.

data_quality_notes: This is the v2 rerun of payload 108. The v1 files (cryogenic_sample_preservation_system_payload_108.md and .json) were left unchanged.

Research for v2 used four WebSearch calls and fourteen page reads (WebFetch). Several NASA technical PDFs (Mitchell et al. 2022, Lewis et al. 2023, Calaway and Allen 2011) were returned as binary content and could not be read as text; claims from them rely on the NTRS abstract pages.

Two pages returned HTTP 403 and were not read: a Georgia Tech repository record on cryogenic lunar sample return and a JAXA conference presentation page. A JAXA curation target below -110 C appeared only in a search summary and is not included as a verified value.

The Example 1 values (-150 C lunar samples, -80 C biological samples, 1 to 3 weeks passive stowage, 10 to 90+ days powered stowage, cold interior about 25 x 25 x 66 cm, system mass below 55 kg, readiness by end of 2027) come from secondary summaries and have not been checked against the primary NASA request for information or the SAM.gov notices.
The -85 C figure in the SatNews article is the article author's estimate, not a stated requirement.
The Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility reference is a Wikipedia article read through a fetch summariser. Its statements should be checked against NASA curation documents before use.

No flown, flight-qualified or built lunar cryogenic sample preservation hardware was identified. No mass, dimensions, power, sealing, lifetime or qualification values are given for any verified cryogenic hardware; they are reported as null or as not publicly specified.
No direct image assets were verified. Image arrays are empty and no images were invented.
No lunar landing-site, lander or rover compatibility is asserted, consistent with the deferral of location recommendations.

The catalogue category 'Water, ice and volatile detection' is used exactly as written. The link to volatile-bearing material is functional and inferred from the payload name and sources, not from a category match.
